passage:
Thursday, 11 p.m.
Skipped the seminar again. I got as far as the door, saw the chairs in a circle, and turned back. Ate lunch on the stairs behind the library so nobody would see me eating alone, which is silly, because that's exactly what I was doing. Ira from my class asked if I wanted to be in her group for the project. I said I already had one. I don't. On the walk back I called myself a coward about twenty times. It's week nine and I haven't made one friend. There's a poster outside the mess about the student counselling centre, free and private. I've walked past it every day. Tomorrow I'm going to write down the timings. Maybe even go in.
Yamini

qa.q: Where did Yamini eat lunch?
qa.a: On the stairs behind the library.

qa.q: What does the name-calling on the walk back show about how Yamini feels?
qa.a: Yamini is lonely and harsh with self-criticism, blaming instead of comforting.

qa.q: What step does Yamini plan for tomorrow, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Writing down the counselling centre timings and maybe going in; seeking help early can make a real difference.

qa.q: How might Ira feel after hearing Yamini already had a group?
qa.a: Ira may feel a little rebuffed, not knowing the truth, and might not ask again unless Yamini reaches out.

grounding: A student who skips seminars, eats alone and refuses group work because being watched feels unbearable plans to visit the counselling centre.

passage: In her first semester at the Delhi college, Kashish had a timetable full of seminars and attended almost none. She would sit outside the seminar room, hear the voices, and walk back to the hostel. She ate in her room so no one would watch her eat alone. When the professor split the class into project groups, she emailed to ask if she could work by herself. At night she told herself she was pathetic. Her roommate Lakshmi noticed the unopened textbooks, the empty noodle cups, the way Kashish flinched at a knock. One evening Lakshmi sat on the edge of her bed. 'You don't have to tell me anything. But the student counselling centre is on the second floor of the library, and they're kind. I went last year. I'll walk you there tomorrow if you want.' Kashish stared at the ceiling. Then she said, 'Okay.'

qa.q: Where is the student counselling centre?
qa.a: On the second floor of the library.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling at night?
qa.a: She felt lonely and ashamed, telling herself she was pathetic.

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi's offer well judged?
qa.a: She didn't demand an explanation, shared that she had gone herself, and offered to walk Kashish there, making early help easier to reach.

qa.q: What had Lakshmi noticed about Kashish?
qa.a: The unopened textbooks, the empty noodle cups and the way Kashish flinched at a knock.

grounding: Shows a student who avoids seminars, meals and group work because being watched feels unbearable, and a roommate who points her early to a counsellor.

passage:
'Liz, you've missed three family calls and all your tutorials. Mummy's worried.' Hrithik sat on the end of her hostel bed; he'd taken the early bus from Kottayam.
'I just can't go in. Everyone looks up when the door opens.'
'Since when?'
'Since October. I eat in my room. I said no to the group project. I told the professor I'd do it alone.'
'Do you want to do it alone?'
'No.' Her voice cracked. 'I'm so lonely I talk to the ceiling. And then I tell myself I'm useless.'
Hrithik was quiet. 'That sounds really heavy. I don't think this is something to push through by yourself.'
'What do I do?'
'Your college has a counsellor. Let's email today. Now, even. I'll stay till you've booked it.'
Elizabeth reached for her laptop. 'Stay till I've booked it.'

qa.q: Where had Hrithik come from?
qa.a: Kottayam, on the early bus.

qa.q: How is Elizabeth feeling about college life?
qa.a: She feels deeply lonely and self-critical, telling herself she is useless.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Hrithik to suggest emailing the counsellor right away?
qa.a: Her avoidance had lasted since October and was feeding loneliness and self-criticism; acting early, with him beside her, makes help more likely.

qa.q: What was it like for Hrithik to hear that she talks to the ceiling?
qa.a: Hrithik was likely shocked and worried, which is why he went quiet and then offered to stay until she booked.

grounding: Shows a student who avoids tutorials, meals and group work because being watched feels unbearable, and a brother who helps her seek a counsellor early.

passage: By the middle of second year I had built a very small life. I'm Urmila. I stopped going to seminars because I couldn't bear everyone turning when I spoke. I ate lunch alone on the back stairs of the library. When Mohit asked me to join his project group, I said I preferred working alone. I didn't. I was lonely in a way that sat on my chest like a weight, and every night I listed my failures. What changed was a poster outside the canteen: 'Feeling stuck? Talk to us.' I walked past it eleven times. The twelfth time, I went in. The counsellor didn't tell me to just be confident. We started tiny: one seminar, sitting by the door. I wish I'd gone in first year. It would have saved me a lot of lonely lunches.

qa.q: What did the poster outside the canteen say?
qa.a: 'Feeling stuck? Talk to us.'

qa.q: How did Urmila feel during second year?
qa.a: Urmila felt lonely, like a weight on the chest, and self-critical, listing failures every night.

qa.q: What does Urmila wish, and why does it matter?
qa.a: To have seen the counsellor in first year; getting help early would have shortened the lonely months.

qa.q: How might Mohit have read 'I preferred working alone'?
qa.a: Mohit probably took it at face value, not knowing Urmila wanted to join but was afraid of being watched.

grounding: Shows a student whose fear of being watched led to skipped seminars, lonely lunches and self-criticism, and the difference a counsellor made.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Girls' Block B, October.
Amandeep has missed four seminars this month. Her roommate, Afreen, came to my office on Monday, worried. "She eats alone in the room. She said group work makes her feel like everyone is staring."
I went up that evening. Amandeep was sitting at her desk with a cold plate beside her. She said, "I'm useless at this college. I can't even sit in a room with people." She sounded very alone.
I didn't tell her to just try harder. I said, "It sounds exhausting, and you shouldn't have to carry it by yourself."
What I did next: with her agreement, I called the campus counsellor that same evening, and she has an appointment on Wednesday. I thanked Afreen for telling me. I will check on Amandeep at dinner each day this week.

qa.q: How many seminars has Amandeep missed this month?
qa.a: Four seminars.

qa.q: How was Amandeep feeling when the warden visited?
qa.a: She felt lonely and ashamed of herself, calling herself useless and saying she couldn't even sit in a room with people.

qa.q: Why was calling the counsellor the same evening a wise step?
qa.a: Her avoidance and self-criticism were growing, and getting a counsellor involved early can make a real difference before things build further.

qa.q: What was it like for Afreen to watch Amandeep eat alone?
qa.a: Afreen was worried enough to go to the warden, and may have felt helpless until an adult stepped in.

grounding: Shows a warden seeing a student avoid seminars and meals because being watched feels unbearable, and linking her to a counsellor early.
